title: Harnessing Van Hove singularities for terahertz photoresponse via Fermi surface reconstruction in kagome lattices

paper_content.abstract: The trihexagonal tiling system exhibits strong electron-electron interactions, positioning it as a key condensed matter platform for studying geometrically frustrated lattices made up of corner-sharing triangles. Its phase-transition-driven lattice modulations enable Fermi surface reconstruction, while emergent van Hove singularities near the Fermi level and correlated band anomalies present critical challenges in understanding electronic interaction mechanisms. By combining temperature-dependent spectroscopy, angle-resolved photoemission, and density functional theory calculations, we demonstrate a 61-fold enhancement in terahertz direct detection mode, ultra-low noise (1.38×10⁻²⁵ A²/Hz) below phase transition temperature, and broadband operation up to 100 GHz in beat-note heterodyne mode. These results are directly correlated with the Fermi surface reconstruction induced by phase transitions. This work positions geometrically frustrated lattices as a powerful platform for studying correlated quantum phenomena, offering new pathways for the design of advanced quantum devices.
paper_content.introduction:
The geometrically frustrated lattice, a network of corner-sharing triangles, represents a foundational platform in condensed matter physics for hosting a spectrum of exotic quantum states. It normally causes Fermi surface reconstruction coupled with singularities in the electronic band structure at the Fermi level (E F). These diverse quantum states include: charge density wave (CDW), spin-liquid states, orbital magnetism, pair density wave (PDW), and unconventional superconductivity. Van Hove singularity (VHS) can drive diverse quantum phenomena; however, their implications for responses to different types of electromagnetic probes (e.g., light) remain underexplored. VHS near the E F can be achieved through graphene-based Moiré superlattices. Current fabrication strategies for advanced optoelectronic devices, which rely heavily on mechanical stacking and chemical vapor deposition (CVD) techniques, face significant limitations that hinder the development of robust and scalable applications. In contrast, VHS can naturally occur in kagome lattices, providing a compelling alternative platform. By harnessing VHS-dominated optoelectronic transitions, such platforms offer a viable pathway for next-generation quantum applications.

The discovered family of materials AV₃Sb₅ (A=K, Rb, Cs), which crystallizes in the hexagonal space group P6/mmm, provides an ideal platform for investigating correlated quantum phenomena. The novel physical properties of the AV₃Sb₅ family have been extensively investigated. Recent breakthroughs include mechanistic studies of superconductivity in CsV₃Sb₅, novel perspectives on symmetry breaking from KV₃Sb₅ research, and laser-STM demonstrations of strain-mediated symmetry control in RbV₃Sb₅ (RVS). The density of states (DOS) at 2D VHS exhibits logarithmic divergence at saddle points while remaining non-divergent at band extrema. This establishes the fundamental importance of VHS in kagome material research. Undoubtedly, the integration of low-energy photon detection techniques enables deeper exploration of VHS in the band structure near the E F of kagome materials. This approach offers unique insights into the distinctive electronic phenomena associated with kagome metals.

In this study, we systematically investigate the low-energy photon detection mechanism in kagome materials through a combined approach of variable-temperature measurements, band-structure observations, and first-principles calculations. By constructing symmetry-engineered electrode antennas on hexagonal lattices, we demonstrate a remarkable nonlinear enhancement in photoresponse under low-energy photon excitation at varying frequencies, mediated by VHS near the E F in RVS. Our custom-designed cryogenic temperature system enables direct observation of VHS-governed exotic phenomena through low-energy direct/beat-note heterodyne configurations. The device exhibits exceptional performance across microwave to terahertz (THz) frequencies, achieving: 61-fold photoresponse enhancement in direct detection mode, ultra-low noise (1.38×10⁻²⁵ A²/Hz) below phase transition temperature (T CDW), broadband operation up to 100 GHz in beat-note heterodyne mode. These results establish a direct correlation between VHS at the E F and light-matter interactions, and elucidate the intrinsic photodetection mechanisms in kagome materials. This work not only provides fundamental understanding of the pivotal role of VHS in governing the extraordinary optoelectronic properties of quantum kagome systems, but also underpins a technical landscape of a kagome material as a universal building block for sensing and energy-harvesting systems that become increasingly ubiquitous nowadays in the studied frequency range.
paper_content.results:
VHS-driven photodetection mechanism
RVS system consists of planar V-atom kagome networks, intervening Sb honeycomb layers, and triangular Rb-ion planes separating the V-Sb slabs. RVS undergoes a CDW phase transition at T CDW (~102 K), which is accompanied by substantial electronic band structure reconstruction, building upon prior research on kagome systems. Figure 1b, c illustrate three key electronic band features of an ideal kagome lattice at the normal state: (i) Dirac cones at the K point, (ii) VHS at the M point, and (iii) momentum-space flat bands. Figure 1d, e illustrate the unit cell configurations of RVS in the normal state and CDW state, respectively. The CDW transition in RVS, within a simple planar case, yields a 2×2 long-range charge ordering pattern, causing an Inverse Star of David (ISD) structure in the plane characterized by a doubling of the primitive cell. Figure 1f presents the electronic band structure at the normal state computed along the Γ-K-M-Γ symmetry line, revealing the predicted pair of VHSs flanking E F near the M point (designated as VHS1 and VHS2 in Fig. 1f). The VHS1 and VHS2 near the E F exhibit complementary dispersion relations—electron-like along Γ-M and hole-like along M-K. This generates a divergent DOS, as confirmed by our calculations. Utilizing the divergent DOS at VHS, we demonstrate photoelectric conversion across both normal and CDW phases (Fig. 1g). Notably, upon entering the CDW state (T<T CDW), the VHS near the M point progressively shifts away from the E F (Fig. S7). This unique VHS redistribution provides a well-defined mechanism for photoresponse enhancement of non-equilibrium carrier transition probabilities (Fig. 1g), which is systematically analyzed in subsequent sections.

Singular electronic band behavior in RbV₃Sb₅
To elucidate the photoelectric detection mechanisms in RVS, we perform density functional theory (DFT) calculations and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) observations (Methods). Our comparative analysis between theoretical and experimental results elucidate the emergence of VHS3 in the CDW phase. The exceptional crystalline quality of the material (detailed in Supplementary Note 1) ensures experimental reproducibility. Figure 2a presents the temperature-dependent in-plane resistivity of RVS, revealing a distinct anomaly at approximately 102 K. This feature is characteristic of a CDW phase transition, consistent with established observations in correlated electron systems. As established in prior investigations, the T CDW exhibits pronounced thickness dependence in AV₃Sb₅ materials. Our systematic study employs an approximately 140 nm-thick sample—a dimensionality carefully selected to maintain bulk-like electronic properties while avoiding the 3D-to-2D crossover regime. Additionally, our results reveal that the pristine phase exhibits marked structural instability. Phonon spectrum, performed on a 3×3×1 supercell, reveals significant phonon mode softening around the M and L points of the Brillouin zone (BZ) boundary in the RVS phonon dispersion (Fig. 2b), unambiguously indicating inherent structural instability in the pristine phase. This lattice dynamical instability serves as the driving mechanism for the CDW phase transition.

By combining theoretical and experimental results, we focus our investigation on a unique feature in the electronic band structure: VHS. Figure 2c displays the DFT-derived electronic structure of RVS, showing orbital-projected (V 3d, Sb 5p) band dispersions in the primitive lattice with (colored) and without (gray) spin-orbit coupling (SOC). Three key characteristics are observed: (i) a dispersionless band across nearly the whole BZ at 1.00±0.05 eV above E F, (ii) Γ-centered electron pockets and Dirac cones dominated by V 3d states near the K point, and (iii) multiple VHSs near M (black arrows) arising from V 3d-Sb 5p hybridization. The VHS1 and VHS2 are particularly significant, positioned within 10 meV of E F and exhibiting complementary dispersion relations—electron-like along Γ-M and hole-like along M-K. This generates a divergent DOS, as confirmed by our calculations.

For low-energy photon detection, we systematically investigate the VHS near the E F in the normal phase and CDW phase. Calculated and ARPES-measured band structures along the high-symmetry paths demonstrate exceptional consistency (Fig. 2d, e). Despite thermal broadening effects at elevated temperatures, we identify two pivotal phenomena: (i) a well-defined hole-like band dispersion along the K-M high-symmetry path, and (ii) the dominant contribution of V d-orbital states to the formation of the VHS. VHS1 manifests hallmark VHS characteristics, exhibiting contrasting dispersion relations along the M–Γ (upward) and M–K (downward) directions. This characteristic leads to a pronounced DOS peak near E F. Figure 2f, g respectively show the theoretically predicted band structure of the ISD state and corresponding ARPES measurements (T<T CDW). The strongly dispersive band along the K-M undergoes a significant downward shift (~0.14 eV at the M point) relative to the normal state, thereby forming a distinct VHS1.

Intriguingly, near the midpoint of the M-K trajectory, the V d-orbital hybridization shows discontinuity and a CDW gap is open. Correspondingly, the part of the band below the E F also undergoes a downward shift, moving entirely below E F. This is clearly captured at ~0.09 eV below E F in the low-temperature experimental results. More intriguingly, a new VHS configuration emerges here, characterized by a hole-like pocket along the M-K direction and an electron-like pocket in the perpendicular direction. A detailed analysis of the band structure at T CDW (Fig. 2h, second-derivative plot along the Γ-K-M-Γ) reveals a new VHS3 (~0.09 eV below E F) near the M-K midpoint (pink marker).

To further verify the characteristics and momentum location of VHS3, Fig. 2i demonstrates exceptional consistency between cryogenic temperature DFT calculations and cryogenic temperature ARPES-derived Fermi surfaces, featuring spectral cuts (1-5) at discrete k x positions along the K-M-K path. A systematic examination through ARPES cuts (Fig. 2i, j) unambiguously establishes the saddle-point character of VHS3. The data show that the band maintains an electron-like dispersion along k y (yellow dashes) at all k x positions, while hole band features (green dashes) with varying k x, which confirms the saddle point. The temperature evolution of the electronic band structure along the K-M-Γ path is annotated in Fig. S7. The downward shift of the V d bands and the formation of new VHS lead to a high DOS crossing the E F, thus leading to electronic structure instability. The calculated DOS exhibits robust agreement with the experimental findings. In both the normal state and CDW state, the DOS exhibits a peak at the saddle point due to the accumulation of occupied states where the electronic band dispersion exhibits a vanishing group velocity (detailed in Supplementary Note 4). Additionally, while the in-plane orbital-dominated Dirac bands near K remain essentially unaffected, the Γ-point electron pocket—composed primarily of out-of-plane p z orbitals—exhibits a pronounced energy shift. This collective behavior provides definitive evidence for a temperature-driven phase transition with Fermi surface reconstruction. These findings demonstrate that VHSs emerge from band structure extrema and saddle points occur at strategic locations that fundamentally govern optoelectronic response.

VHS-governed exotic phenomena through direct configurations
Our analysis reveals that RVS undergoes significant topological modifications near its T CDW, manifesting as band structure evolution, Fermi surface reconstruction, and pronounced VHS rearrangements. These emergent properties create unprecedented opportunities for low-energy photon detection. Our work demonstrates—for the first time—the direct utilization of kagome-derived topological states for photodetection. We now present the remarkably promising experimental results in photodetection.

We develop the structure of the kagome-metal-based photodetector (Fig. 3a), comprising a bowtie antenna-which serves as electrodes and features a left-right symmetric optical field efficiently coupling photon energy into the channel-and the kagome material RVS. The RVS channel layer is prepared by mechanical exfoliation, and the device is meticulously patterned into a planar configuration. (further details are provided in the Methods). Complete finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulation details are provided in Supplementary Note 5.

The energy distribution curves (EDCs) extracted near the E F region (Fig. 3b) demonstrate the dynamic evolution of the RVS system’s band structure with decreasing temperature (from 130 to 10.5 K). In the normal state (T>T CDW), both VHS1 and VHS2 at the M-point maintain their positions and exhibit minimal temperature dependence. In the CDW state (T<T CDW), the electronic states near the M-point undergo a progressive shift toward higher binding energies with decreasing temperature (further details illustrated in Fig. S7). In kagome systems exhibiting Fermi surface nesting characteristics, these observations provide key insights into the microscopic physical mechanisms underlying electronic instabilities. The VHS exhibits intrinsic electronic instability. Fermi surface nesting facilitates enhanced electron scattering along its characteristic wavevector. Simultaneously, the emergence of a new VHS3 feature leads to a significant amplification of the DOS at the E F. The strongly enhanced DOS at these singularities creates ideal conditions for low-energy photon detection. Figure 3c elucidates the microscopic mechanism governing the enhanced photoresponse, showing that the VHS-induced DOS peak increases the number of available initial states for the optical transition.

Our full-spectrum analysis reveals distinct temperature-dependent photoresponse characteristics of the photodetector across three key THz bands (0.02–0.04, 0.08–0.1, and 0.33–0.355 THz) at 0 mV bias. Figure 3d–f demonstrate that the photoresponse intensity, color-graded from dark to light blue (strongest to weakest), consistently peaks at T CDW ~102 K in all frequency ranges. The top-view schematics (Fig. 3d–f, insets) spatially resolve these response maxima. As the photocurrent intensity exhibits a positive correlation with the DOS, we derive the quantitative relationship expressed in Eq. 1.

J(ω) ∝ e D(E) |⟨f| H^ int |i⟩|² ℏω Φ(ω) (1)

where J(ω) denotes photocurrent density, e represents electron charge, D(E) corresponds to the electronic DOS, ⟨f| H^ int |i⟩ describes transition matrix element incorporating initial state, final state, and perturbation Hamiltonian, ℏω is incident photon energy, Φ(ω) describes incident photon flux. As clearly demonstrated by the simplified Eq. 1, the photocurrent density is directly influenced by the electronic DOS. In the normal state of kagome metal RVS, two VHSs exist near the E F at the high-symmetry M-point. CDW phase transition renormalizes the band structure and new VHS emerges. Since the electronic DOS exhibits logarithmic divergence near VHS, the phase transition therefore enhances the photocurrent density J(ω) through increased D(E).

Under an applied bias of 100 mV, we systematically measured the temperature-dependent photoresponse of the RVS-based detector at 0.03, 0.09, and 0.35 THz (Fig. 3g). Experimental results indicate that at T CDW (~102 K), the device’s photoresponse exhibits significant nonlinear enhancement. Notably, applying a 100 mV bias maintains the peak frequency while significantly enhancing the photocurrent intensity (full spectral scans available in Supplementary Note 8). This enhancement mechanism arises from bias-excited electronic transitions between VHS.

Figure 3h compares the photoresponse enhancement between the normal and CDW phases at a 100 mV bias, revealing frequency-dependent amplification factors of 60.82 × (0.03 THz); 12.64 × (0.1 THz); and 3.18 × (0.35 THz). This enhancement aligns with the theoretical predictions: the phase transition redistributes VHS and modifies the electronic DOS near critical points, thereby amplifying interband transitions. Our results establish kagome materials as a platform for frequency-selective photoresponses through many-body correlations.

The second-order photocurrent (I ph) scaled linearly with the incident electric field power (P in) across temperatures (77–300 K), as shown in Fig. 3i. The photodetector exhibits ideal linearity over more than two orders of magnitude in P in and the data are well fitted with a simple power law (I ph ∝ P in^α, α=0.99±0.005) at all measured temperatures. This temperature-independent nonlinearity is a direct manifestation of the RVS system’s singularelectronic structure, where VHS-derived DOS enhances multiphoton processes. Our results establish kagome materials as a unique platform for wide-temperature-range nonlinear photonics.

Noise is a critical parameter influencing the performance of optoelectronic devices. Once the temperature is below T CDW, the electronic noise spectral density shows a dramatic reduction by over two orders of magnitude (from 3.8×10⁻²³ A²/Hz² to 1.38×10⁻²⁵ A²/Hz²). The system exhibits enhanced stability upon entering the CDW state, with significantly reduced random carrier scattering events. The Noise Equivalent Power (NEP) is a critical parameter. Across the entire modulation frequency range, the device achieves an average NEP of approximately 20 pW/Hz¹/². Operating at 0.1 THz, our device demonstrates ultrafast response characteristics with 580 ns rise time and 520 ns fall time, which is several orders of magnitude faster than other thermoelectric detectors (such as ≈ 170 µs of tellurium nanowire photodetector). (see details in Fig. S12)

VHS-driven heterodyne mixing from millimeter wave to THz band
Based on the unique VHS properties as well as band-renormalization of kagome-metals, we further investigate the potential of heterodyne detection. In our measurements (details can be found in Methods), the fabricated kagome material-based mixer serves as a frequency conversion device in the circuit (Fig. 4a), which constitutes a critical component in modern RF communication systems.

The heterodyne THz detection system, governed by novel physical mechanisms, achieves broadband operation and high detection sensitivity across phase transitions. The schematic illustration of the mixing process under optical beating with in two different frequencies in kagome-based materials is presented in Fig. 4b. The kagome material-based mixer generates distinctive heterodyne signals through coupling of the local oscillator (f LO) and radio frequency (f RF) inputs, yielding an intermediate-frequency beat signal V IF described by:

V IF(t) = L 0(t) R THz(t) = L o R THz/2 * cos(ω LO - ω THz)t + cos(ω LO + ω THz)t (2)

where V IF(t) represents the intermediate frequency output signal, L 0(t) represents the local oscillator signal, R THz(t) represents the radio frequency signal. First, we demonstrate harmonic mixing in a kagome material-based mixer under collimated 6.5 GHz excitation. Through spectrum analysis, the first, second, and third harmonic comb lines are clearly resolved, with the harmonic signals exhibiting robust power dependence. Notably, the generated frequency comb also serves as a tunable local oscillator (f LO), enabling versatile heterodyne mixing. The measured f IF adheres precisely to the expected relationship: f IF = f RF – n f LO (n∈ℕ+) (Figure S14).

Through temperature-dependent measurements, we implement heterodyne mixing techniques in kagome-material-based mixers to systematically investigate their potential for modern communication technologies. Figure 4c demonstrates the temperature evolution of f IF signal arising from the distinctive VHS inherent to kagome systems. To ensure reliable characterization of mixing dynamics within the spectrum analyzer’s bandwidth constraints, we implement a heterodyne scheme using 22.4 GHz (f LO) and 23.4 GHz (f RF) signals. Control experiments with three independent mixers confirmed the reproducibility of our observations. Notably, we observe a pronounced enhancement in f IF signal intensity as the temperature decreased from 300 K to below T CDW. This anomalous behavior originates from temperature-induced modifications in the electronic band structure: (i) the emergence and upward energy shift of a VHS at the M-point, and (ii) the formation of a secondary VHS at the R-point below T CDW. The cooperative migration of these singularities enhances electronic transitions, resulting in the observed macroscopic amplification of the f IF signal.

Kagome systems exhibit exceptional promise for self-mixing applications as noted above. Building on this foundation, we observe broadband multi-wave-mixing in nonlinear kagome systems. Figure 4d demonstrates the characteristic signatures of subharmonic N-wave mixing (WM) (f LO is 23.4 GHz, f RF is 25.4 GHz and f IF signal is precisely captured by the spectrum analyzer). These peaks include three types of spectra: the two fundamental signals (ω₁=2πf LO, ω₂=2πf RF), the f IF signal (f IF = f RF - f LO), their higher-order modes, and the WM components (n f LO ± m f RF, where n, m=1, 2, 3…). The highest observed components reach up to 5 (f RF - f LO) and 6 f LO - 5f RF. These results indicate that, due to the material’s highly complex Fermi surface and exotic electronic behavior below T CDW, a frequency comb-like heterodyne mixing effect can be generated, with higher-order components extending up to the fifth order.

To further investigate the dynamic range of the kagome material-based mixer, the relationship between the f IF signals of different harmonic mixing orders and the incident power (P LO and P RF) is shown in Fig. 4e. The relationship follows the power law, P out = α P in (where P in = P RF), and the solid line represents the slope of the output power measured in the experiment. Notably, even when the f IF signal is set to its lower limit (P RF = -25 dBm, P LO = 14.8 dBm), the f IF signals at (f RF - f LO) and (2f LO - f RF) remain clearly detectable. This indicates that the minimum power excitation threshold of the mixer can be less than -25 dBm, demonstrating the potential of kagome materials for precise carrier frequency information acquisition.

By harnessing the exotic electronic properties of kagome material, we demonstrate the mixing range to the THz band for modern RF communication systems. The f LO is increased to above 100 GHz, approaching the electrical oscillation limit of micron-scale devices. Simultaneously, the f RF is tuned across a range from the Ku and Ka bands to the W band, as shown in Fig. 4f. This shows that the kagome-based device demonstrates intrinsic frequency-agile capture capability, operating across a very wide bandwidth of 1–100 GHz. The conversion loss (CL) increases from 20.1 ± 0.2 dB to 57.5 ± 0.2 dB at 100 GHz. This performance highlights the device’s promising applicability in next-generation wireless communication systems.

The frequency CL, defined as one of the key metrics for mixers, is expressed as:

CL = P in / P out = 10 log (30 P RF / P IF) (3)

where, 30 represents the gain coefficient of the LNA, S λ=λ²/4π represents the diffraction-limited area within the incident wavelength; S represents the area of the waveguide flare. The CL of the mixer near 100 GHz is 57.5 ± 2 dB, while the CL in the RF band is 20 ± 2 dB.
paper_content.methods:
Crystal growth and characterization
Single crystals of RbV₃Sb₅ were grown via flux-based growth technique. The precursor RbSb was prepared by reacting Rb (purity 99.75%) and Sb granules (purity 99.99%) at 300 °C. Starting materials of RbSb, Sb and V powder (purity 99.99%) were loaded inside a Canfield crucible with a molar ratio of 3:9:1, sealed in a quartz tube. The assembly was heated up to 1100 °C in a furnace within 12 h and kept at this temperature for 10 h. It was subsequently slowly cooled down to 800 °C at a temperature decreasing rate of 50 °C/h and kept for 5 h, and then slowly cooled down further to 450 °C at 2 °C/h. Finally, the assembly was taken out from the furnace and decanted with a centrifuge to separate RbV₃Sb₅ single crystal from the flux. With the exception of sealing and heat treatment procedures, all other preparation processes were conducted in an argon-filled glove box to prevent reaction of Rb with atmospheric oxygen and moisture.

Atomically resolved the scanning transmission electron microscope measurement
The atomic arrangement was examined using a double aberration-corrected Thermo Scientific Spectra 300 STEM (Thermo Scientific, USA), operating at 300 kV with a convergence angle of 25 mrad and a collection angle ranging from 70 to 250 mrad. HAADF STEM images were acquired with a dwell time of 10 s per pixel.

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy measurement
ARPES was used to characterize kagome metal RbV₃Sb₅ samples. The ARPES measurements were conducted at the BL-03U beamline of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility, using a Scienta Omicron DA30 analyzer. The photon energy is 86 eV. The energy and angular resolutions were set to better than 50 meV and 0.02 Å⁻¹, respectively. Samples were cleaved in situ under ultrahigh vacuum conditions, revealing flat and mirror-like (100) surfaces. During measurements, the temperature was maintained at T~9 K, and the pressure in the main chamber was kept below 7×10⁻¹¹ torr.

First-principles calculations and theoretical modeling
We performed first-principles calculations using the Vienna ab initio simulation package with the projector augmented-wave method. The exchange-correlation energy was treated with the generalized-gradient approximation functional of Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof. The plane-wave basis was employed with a kinetic-energy cutoff of 600 eV, and the k-space integration was performed with 9×9×4 and 4×4×4 k-meshes for the pristine cell and 2×2×1 supercell, respectively. All atoms were allowed to relax along the calculated forces until all the residual force components were less than 0.001 eV/Å. The calculated lattice parameters of the pristine structure are a=b=5.472 and c=9.073 Å. The spectral function A(k, E F) on the Fermi Surface was computed using WANNIER90 and WANNIERTOOLS, where the maximally localized Wannier functions were constructed by projecting the Bloch states onto V-d and Sb-p atomic orbitals. The phonon spectrum for the pristine phase was calculated using the finite displacement method with 3×3×4 k-points and a 3×3×1 supercell.

Device fabrication
Under room temperature conditions, optoelectronic devices were fabricated through mechanical exfoliation. The high-quality RbV₃Sb₅ sample was mechanically exfoliated onto blue tape (Shanghai Onway Technology Co., Ltd) and then directly transferred onto a high-resistivity silicon (ρ=20,000 Ω·cm) substrate coated with a thin SiO₂ oxide layer (300 nm), resulting in an RbV₃Sb₅ thin film. The antenna structure was patterned, and the contact area was defined using electron beam lithography, followed by etching. Cr/Au was deposited onto the material via electron beam evaporation to establish the electrical contact. The optoelectronic detector was fabricated following the metal lift-off process.

Performance measurement
The electrical characteristics of the detector at room temperature were obtained using a Keithley 4200A-SCS Parametric Analyzer. For optical measurements, the THz frequency was tuned to 0.30 THz (WR 2.8 tripler) and 0.12 THz (WR 9 tripler) using a VDI multiplier connected to a 40 GHz microwave source (Agilent E8257D). The optical response was modulated with a TTL signal at a frequency of 1 kHz and recorded using an oscilloscope, after passing through a low-noise voltage preamplifier (SR570) and a lock-in amplifier (SR830). The power density of the THz radiation was measured using a commercially calibrated photomixing THz power meter (TK100), with measurements taken at 2.5, 1, and 1 mW cm⁻² for frequencies of 0.04, 0.12, and 0.30 THz, respectively.

Heterodyne-mixing characterizations
A heterodyne is a signal frequency that is created by combining or mixing two other frequencies using a signal processing technique called heterodyning, which was invented by Canadian inventor-engineer Reginald Fessenden. Heterodyne mixing can be understood by analogy to musical beats-when two slightly different musical notes are played simultaneously, we hear a pulsating ‘beat’ at the difference frequency between them. Similarly, in heterodyne mixing, two signals at different frequencies (local oscillator and radio frequency) are combined in a nonlinear device (the mixer), producing new signals at the sum (f RF + f LO) and difference (|f RF - f LO|) frequencies. In our measurements, the fabricated mixer (kagome material-based detector) serves as a frequency conversion device within the circuit (Fig. 4a), constituting a critical component in modern RF communication systems. The differential frequency (referred to as the intermediate frequency) is selectively utilized because it enables easier electronic processing compared to the original high-frequency signal.

The mixing system at cryogenic temperature primarily consists of two major modules: the heterodyne mixing optical path and the cryogenic temperature refrigeration system. As shown in the lower-left part of the Fig. 4a, the system includes essential components for modern wireless communication—the f LO signal and the heterodyne f RF signal. The f LO signal is collimated using a TPX (polymethylpentene) lens with a focal length of 100 mm and directed onto a beam splitter. The f RF signal is incident on the beam splitter via an off-axis parabolic mirror (OAP), which focuses the millimeter-wave/THz beam. The optical signal is then precisely combined and directed onto the mixer after passing through the Dewar window (Sapphire). Different frequency bands requires specific THz sources. For microwave mixing in the 0–67 GHz range, a microwave source (Agilent E8257D, 0.02–0.04 THz) and a vector network analyzer (Ceyear) are used to provide the f LO and f RF signals, respectively. For the mixing configuration in the 0.08–0.12 THz range, the Agilent E8257D microwave source (0.02–0.04 THz) is connected to a VDI multiplier (WR 9.0) and a 100 GHz source (TeraSense). The f IF is fed into a LNA (ultra wide band=0.01–20 GHz, gain=30 dB Typ, noise figure=2.5 dB). The amplified f IF signal was then measured using a spectrum analyzer (0–27 GHz). Meanwhile, the other path of the optical signal passing through the beam splitter is accurately directed onto a TK power meter to calibrate the optical power. The right half of the figure depicts the low-temperature refrigeration module, which comprises a 77 K Closed Cycle Cryogenic System manufactured by Shanghai Lind Precision Instruments Limited.

In the higher-order harmonic mixing section, the f LO signal is used to generate higher-order harmonics signals (n f LO, where n ranges from 1 to 6) at the point of incidence. These generated signals are then mixed with another RF signal to produce an IF signal, denoted as (n f LO - f RF).

Data availability
Relevant data generated in this study are provided in the article and Supplementary Information. All raw data that support the plots within this paper and other findings of this study are available from the corresponding authors upon request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have successfully developed a low-energy photon detector based on a Kagome material. Using ARPES on RVS, they observe an electronic phase transition below TCDW​ that brings van Hove singularities (VHS) close to the Fermi level. They demonstrate the critical role of VHS in driving electronic instability and related exotic phenomena, reporting a substantial enhancement in photoresponse by a factor of 62. However, several points require clarification, particularly regarding the ARPES and DFT results and the link between VHS and the enhanced photoresponse, before the manuscript can be considered for publication:
1) As the authors note in the introduction, VHS are expected to show a logarithmically divergent DOS, similar to what was observed in twisted bilayer graphene by D. Marchenko et al. (Sci. Adv. 4, eaau0059 (2018)).
a) The manuscript claims that DFT calculations confirm a divergent DOS, yet no such figure is presented in the main text. Possibly this refers to Supplementary Figure S6?
b) Even in that supplementary figure, there does not appear to be a logarithmic divergence where the VHS is expected. Rather, the peak shown resembles a standard DOS maximum typical of any band edge. The same observation holds for the experimental EDCs. Could the authors clarify?
c) Are the EDCs integrated over the full momentum space? If so, it might be more informative to integrate only over regions near the VHS bands, to minimize contributions from other bands at similar energies.
d) Regarding the DFT DOS, is the integration performed over the entire Brillouin zone? It would be helpful to see how the DOS behaves specifically along the Γ-M-K directions.
e) Including these figures in the main text rather than in the supplementary materials would improve the clarity and impact of the discussion.
2) It would be beneficial if the authors could provide constant energy contour (CEC) plots at the Fermi level, both below and above TCDW​, to more clearly illustrate the reported Fermi surface reconstruction.
3) Colorbars are missing in most panels of Figure 2.
4) At line 155, the authors state that a distinct hole-like band along K–M flattens at binding energies below 0.3 eV. This feature is not readily apparent in the figures. Could they specify where this band is located?
5) The downward shift of the VHS3 band with decreasing temperature is noted, and the authors suggest this leads to a high DOS at the Fermi level, causing electronic instability. Further elaboration on the physical mechanism behind this instability would be appreciated.
6) Based on the data, it appears that VHS1 and VHS2 shift downward upon the phase transition, and there is a subsequent change in the dispersion of VHS2, which the authors later refer to as VHS3. Is this interpretation accurate?

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors explore the possibility of utilizing the Fermi surface reconstruction associated with charge-density wave transitions in 2D van-der-Waals materials - specifically in the V-based kagome metal RbV3Sb5 - for photo-sensoric devices. Via ARPES and DFT calculations, they recall and highlight the temperature-dependent changes in the electronic band structure, with an emphasis on a van-Hove singularity close to the Fermi level. Exploiting these Fermi-surface features, they demonstrate a photocurrent detection capabilities of a RbV3Sb5-based detector device.
While this work tackles an underexplored aspect of kagome metals which may open the door to future applications, there are several issues that deserve attention, clarification, and improvement before considering the manuscript for publication.
- The authors assume an inverse-Star-of-David as the CDW pattern in RbV3Sb5. As far as I understand, the precise pattern is still an open issue (although recent works seem to slightly favor an inverse-Star-of-David over a star-of-David pattern). Can the authors elaborate on their assumption? I suggest they also plot the electronic band structure for a star-of-David pattern for comparison and comment on the fundamental differences between those two (if any).
- Related to the former comment is the issue of potential stacking faults, which are known to occur in V-based kagome materials depending on the cleavage procedure as well as the cooling rate. The authors should discuss these potential effects, as they may be highly relevant for future fabrication and application processes.
- In Fig. 2a, the resistivity curves from three different samples show transition temperatures between 92 K and 102 K. Meanwhile, the authors emphasize an "outstanding single-crystal quality". Please discuss in the manuscript the potential origin of the wide range of transition temperatures.
- The authors also speculate about softening of acoustic modes "possibly evidencing a structural instability" - there have been numerous studies detailing el-el and el-ph coupling, and the role of crystal structure on the CDW formation AV3Sb5, so I don't get why the authors need to describe it in these vague terms. Better to add some relevant references at this point.
- I find some of the phrasing related to the ARPES results somewhat confusing. I get that the authors want to present their ARPES results to link features of the electronic band structure to photo-sensoric activity of RbV3Sb5. However, in my view the electronic (CDW) phase transition has been heavily studied and well-established for years. Yet, parts of the text read as if nothing is known so far about the electronic structure. Take for example: "Compelling evidence of electronic phase transitions in Kagome materials". Am I missing some newly uncovered observation made by the authors for the first time? Otherwise, these ARPES results do not report any novel discovery or observation, hence there is no need to present them as "compelling evidence".
- Finally, I would like to see a comparison of the photo-sensoric performance of RbV3Sb5 with other related vdW materials, as well as with other, conventional materials in the discussion, so that the readers may better appreciate the performance. Likewise, can the authors comment on potentially utilizing other CDW materials with a transition temperature closer to room temperature? Are there any fundamental advantages of V-based kagome metals?
Minor issues:
- Abstract: "enhancement in in terahertz"
- Line 45: Add a reference at the end of the first sentence.
- Line 47: Ref. 1 does not seem to be a proper, primary reference here.
- Line 106: specify the value of T_CDW, add a reference at the end of the sentence.
- "Notably, upon entering the CDW phase (T < TCDW), the VHS near the M point progressively shifts away from the EF, while a new VHS forms at the R point.": mark and illustrate these changes in Fig. 1 as well.
- Lines 241-243 and lines 249-250 are nearly identical.
- Since Fig. 3b only contains 5 curves, it might be advantageous to simply plot all curves on top of each other to better appreciate the changes through the transition temperature.

1) TiSe₂:
ARPES and first-principles calculations reveal that bulk TiSe₂ undergoes a CDW

2) CuTe:
CuTe exhibits a CDW transition temperature of 300 K under hydrostatic pressure

necessity for sustained high-pressure conditions poses challenges for practical detector

3) TaS₂:
TaS₂ exhibits characteristic CDW sliding behavior, with a CDW transition
occurring near room temperature (~350 K for the nearly commensurate (NC) phase).
When an external electric field surpasses the threshold for phase excitation modes, the
material displays pronounced nonlinear current-voltage characteristics, marked by an
abrupt resistance drop—a signature of collective CDW depinning.
Notably, sub-threshold optical excitation can modulate the resistive state even
when the applied bias voltage is insufficient to trigger CDW sliding. This effect induces
premature phase-mode sliding, suggesting a light-sensitive control mechanism for
CDW dynamics. Such behavior enables applications in broadband photodetection,
where the RVS mechanism exploits TaS₂’s intrinsic coupling between electronic and
structural orders for optoelectronic response20.
3.Fundamental Advantages of V-Based Kagome Metals
1) Unique Electronic Properties Arising from the Structure of Vanadium-Based
Kagome Metals
The vanadium-based kagome metals, particularly the AV₃Sb₅ (A = K, Rb, Cs)
family, have emerged as an exceptional platform for investigating the interplay of
geometric frustration, electronic correlations, and topological states in quantum
materials. The two-dimensional kagome lattice—composed of corner-sharing
triangles—generates several extraordinary electronic features21:
(1) Dirac Points:
Similar to graphene, the kagome lattice inherently possesses Dirac cones in its
band structure. However, due to the involvement of a three-orbital basis, these cones
exhibit more complex characteristics
(2) Flat Bands:
The strong geometric frustration in the kagome lattice gives rise to completely
dispersionless (flat) electronic bands, significantly enhancing electron correlation
effects.
(3) VHS:
A high density-of-states point in electronic structures induced by lattice geometry,
capable of driving various instabilities.
2) Rich Phase Diagrams with Coexisting Multiple Order Parameters
Vanadium-based kagome metals exhibit exceptionally rich phase diagrams
encompassing multiple competing electronic ordered states:
(1) CDW:
These materials exhibit a CDW transition at relatively high temperatures
(approximately 70–100 K, depending on the A-site element), which is highly unusual
in metallic systems22.
(2) Time-Reversal Symmetry Breaking:
Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and muon spin relaxation (μSR)
experiments reveal time-reversal symmetry breaking below the CDW transition
temperature, suggesting the possible existence of a chiral flux phase or orbital currents23.
(3) Electronic Nematic Phase:
Below the CDW transition temperature, these materials form an electronic nematic
28 / 32
phase that breaks the sixfold rotational symmetry of the kagome lattice.
3) Topologically Nontrivial Unconventional Superconductivity
(1) Strong Coupling:
The ratio of 2Δ/kBTc ≈ 5 in CsV₃Sb₅ indicates that it belongs to the category of
strongly coupled superconductors24.
(2) Pair Density Wave (PDW):
High-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) has revealed a 3Q PDW
state coexisting with superconductivity in CsV₃Sb₅, manifested as spatial modulation
of the superconducting gap. This "roton-PDW" state may be associated with an
underlying vortex-antivortex lattice.
(3) Topological Aspects:
The combination of nontrivial band topology and superconductivity may endow

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The trihexagonal tiling system exhibits strong electron-electron interactions, positioning it as a key condensed matter platform for studying geometrically frustrated lattices made up of corner-sharing triangles. Its phase-transition-driven lattice modulations enable Fermi surface reconstruction, while emergent van Hove singularities near the Fermi level and correlated band anomalies present critical challenges in understanding electronic interaction mechanisms. By combining temperature-dependent spectroscopy, angle-resolved photoemission, and density functional theory calculations, we demonstrate a 61-fold enhancement in terahertz direct detection mode, ultra-low noise (1.38×10⁻²⁵ A²/Hz) below phase transition temperature, and broadband operation up to 100 GHz in beat-note heterodyne mode. These results are directly correlated with the Fermi surface reconstruction induced by phase transitions. This work positions geometrically frustrated lattices as a powerful platform for studying correlated quantum phenomena, offering new pathways for the design of advanced quantum devices.

---

## Introduction

The geometrically frustrated lattice, a network of corner-sharing triangles, represents a foundational platform in condensed matter physics for hosting a spectrum of exotic quantum states. It normally causes Fermi surface reconstruction coupled with singularities in the electronic band structure at the Fermi level (E F). These diverse quantum states include: charge density wave (CDW), spin-liquid states, orbital magnetism, pair density wave (PDW), and unconventional superconductivity. Van Hove singularity (VHS) can drive diverse quantum phenomena; however, their implications for responses to different types of electromagnetic probes (e.g., light) remain underexplored. VHS near the E F can be achieved through graphene-based Moiré superlattices. Current fabrication strategies for advanced optoelectronic devices, which rely heavily on mechanical stacking and chemical vapor deposition (CVD) techniques, face significant limitations that hinder the development of robust and scalable applications. In contrast, VHS can naturally occur in kagome lattices, providing a compelling alternative platform. By harnessing VHS-dominated optoelectronic transitions, such platforms offer a viable pathway for next-generation quantum applications.

The discovered family of materials AV₃Sb₅ (A=K, Rb, Cs), which crystallizes in the hexagonal space group P6/mmm, provides an ideal platform for investigating correlated quantum phenomena. The novel physical properties of the AV₃Sb₅ family have been extensively investigated. Recent breakthroughs include mechanistic studies of superconductivity in CsV₃Sb₅, novel perspectives on symmetry breaking from KV₃Sb₅ research, and laser-STM demonstrations of strain-mediated symmetry control in RbV₃Sb₅ (RVS). The density of states (DOS) at 2D VHS exhibits logarithmic divergence at saddle points while remaining non-divergent at band extrema. This establishes the fundamental importance of VHS in kagome material research. Undoubtedly, the integration of low-energy photon detection techniques enables deeper exploration of VHS in the band structure near the E F of kagome materials. This approach offers unique insights into the distinctive electronic phenomena associated with kagome metals.

In this study, we systematically investigate the low-energy photon detection mechanism in kagome materials through a combined approach of variable-temperature measurements, band-structure observations, and first-principles calculations. By constructing symmetry-engineered electrode antennas on hexagonal lattices, we demonstrate a remarkable nonlinear enhancement in photoresponse under low-energy photon excitation at varying frequencies, mediated by VHS near the E F in RVS. Our custom-designed cryogenic temperature system enables direct observation of VHS-governed exotic phenomena through low-energy direct/beat-note heterodyne configurations. The device exhibits exceptional performance across microwave to terahertz (THz) frequencies, achieving: 61-fold photoresponse enhancement in direct detection mode, ultra-low noise (1.38×10⁻²⁵ A²/Hz) below phase transition temperature (T CDW), broadband operation up to 100 GHz in beat-note heterodyne mode. These results establish a direct correlation between VHS at the E F and light-matter interactions, and elucidate the intrinsic photodetection mechanisms in kagome materials. This work not only provides fundamental understanding of the pivotal role of VHS in governing the extraordinary optoelectronic properties of quantum kagome systems, but also underpins a technical landscape of a kagome material as a universal building block for sensing and energy-harvesting systems that become increasingly ubiquitous nowadays in the studied frequency range.

---

## Results

VHS-driven photodetection mechanism
RVS system consists of planar V-atom kagome networks, intervening Sb honeycomb layers, and triangular Rb-ion planes separating the V-Sb slabs. RVS undergoes a CDW phase transition at T CDW (~102 K), which is accompanied by substantial electronic band structure reconstruction, building upon prior research on kagome systems. Figure 1b, c illustrate three key electronic band features of an ideal kagome lattice at the normal state: (i) Dirac cones at the K point, (ii) VHS at the M point, and (iii) momentum-space flat bands. Figure 1d, e illustrate the unit cell configurations of RVS in the normal state and CDW state, respectively. The CDW transition in RVS, within a simple planar case, yields a 2×2 long-range charge ordering pattern, causing an Inverse Star of David (ISD) structure in the plane characterized by a doubling of the primitive cell. Figure 1f presents the electronic band structure at the normal state computed along the Γ-K-M-Γ symmetry line, revealing the predicted pair of VHSs flanking E F near the M point (designated as VHS1 and VHS2 in Fig. 1f). The VHS1 and VHS2 near the E F exhibit complementary dispersion relations—electron-like along Γ-M and hole-like along M-K. This generates a divergent DOS, as confirmed by our calculations. Utilizing the divergent DOS at VHS, we demonstrate photoelectric conversion across both normal and CDW phases (Fig. 1g). Notably, upon entering the CDW state (T<T CDW), the VHS near the M point progressively shifts away from the E F (Fig. S7). This unique VHS redistribution provides a well-defined mechanism for photoresponse enhancement of non-equilibrium carrier transition probabilities (Fig. 1g), which is systematically analyzed in subsequent sections.

Singular electronic band behavior in RbV₃Sb₅
To elucidate the photoelectric detection mechanisms in RVS, we perform density functional theory (DFT) calculations and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) observations (Methods). Our comparative analysis between theoretical and experimental results elucidate the emergence of VHS3 in the CDW phase. The exceptional crystalline quality of the material (detailed in Supplementary Note 1) ensures experimental reproducibility. Figure 2a presents the temperature-dependent in-plane resistivity of RVS, revealing a distinct anomaly at approximately 102 K. This feature is characteristic of a CDW phase transition, consistent with established observations in correlated electron systems. As established in prior investigations, the T CDW exhibits pronounced thickness dependence in AV₃Sb₅ materials. Our systematic study employs an approximately 140 nm-thick sample—a dimensionality carefully selected to maintain bulk-like electronic properties while avoiding the 3D-to-2D crossover regime. Additionally, our results reveal that the pristine phase exhibits marked structural instability. Phonon spectrum, performed on a 3×3×1 supercell, reveals significant phonon mode softening around the M and L points of the Brillouin zone (BZ) boundary in the RVS phonon dispersion (Fig. 2b), unambiguously indicating inherent structural instability in the pristine phase. This lattice dynamical instability serves as the driving mechanism for the CDW phase transition.

By combining theoretical and experimental results, we focus our investigation on a unique feature in the electronic band structure: VHS. Figure 2c displays the DFT-derived electronic structure of RVS, showing orbital-projected (V 3d, Sb 5p) band dispersions in the primitive lattice with (colored) and without (gray) spin-orbit coupling (SOC). Three key characteristics are observed: (i) a dispersionless band across nearly the whole BZ at 1.00±0.05 eV above E F, (ii) Γ-centered electron pockets and Dirac cones dominated by V 3d states near the K point, and (iii) multiple VHSs near M (black arrows) arising from V 3d-Sb 5p hybridization. The VHS1 and VHS2 are particularly significant, positioned within 10 meV of E F and exhibiting complementary dispersion relations—electron-like along Γ-M and hole-like along M-K. This generates a divergent DOS, as confirmed by our calculations.

For low-energy photon detection, we systematically investigate the VHS near the E F in the normal phase and CDW phase. Calculated and ARPES-measured band structures along the high-symmetry paths demonstrate exceptional consistency (Fig. 2d, e). Despite thermal broadening effects at elevated temperatures, we identify two pivotal phenomena: (i) a well-defined hole-like band dispersion along the K-M high-symmetry path, and (ii) the dominant contribution of V d-orbital states to the formation of the VHS. VHS1 manifests hallmark VHS characteristics, exhibiting contrasting dispersion relations along the M–Γ (upward) and M–K (downward) directions. This characteristic leads to a pronounced DOS peak near E F. Figure 2f, g respectively show the theoretically predicted band structure of the ISD state and corresponding ARPES measurements (T<T CDW). The strongly dispersive band along the K-M undergoes a significant downward shift (~0.14 eV at the M point) relative to the normal state, thereby forming a distinct VHS1.

Intriguingly, near the midpoint of the M-K trajectory, the V d-orbital hybridization shows discontinuity and a CDW gap is open. Correspondingly, the part of the band below the E F also undergoes a downward shift, moving entirely below E F. This is clearly captured at ~0.09 eV below E F in the low-temperature experimental results. More intriguingly, a new VHS configuration emerges here, characterized by a hole-like pocket along the M-K direction and an electron-like pocket in the perpendicular direction. A detailed analysis of the band structure at T CDW (Fig. 2h, second-derivative plot along the Γ-K-M-Γ) reveals a new VHS3 (~0.09 eV below E F) near the M-K midpoint (pink marker).

To further verify the characteristics and momentum location of VHS3, Fig. 2i demonstrates exceptional consistency between cryogenic temperature DFT calculations and cryogenic temperature ARPES-derived Fermi surfaces, featuring spectral cuts (1-5) at discrete k x positions along the K-M-K path. A systematic examination through ARPES cuts (Fig. 2i, j) unambiguously establishes the saddle-point character of VHS3. The data show that the band maintains an electron-like dispersion along k y (yellow dashes) at all k x positions, while hole band features (green dashes) with varying k x, which confirms the saddle point. The temperature evolution of the electronic band structure along the K-M-Γ path is annotated in Fig. S7. The downward shift of the V d bands and the formation of new VHS lead to a high DOS crossing the E F, thus leading to electronic structure instability. The calculated DOS exhibits robust agreement with the experimental findings. In both the normal state and CDW state, the DOS exhibits a peak at the saddle point due to the accumulation of occupied states where the electronic band dispersion exhibits a vanishing group velocity (detailed in Supplementary Note 4). Additionally, while the in-plane orbital-dominated Dirac bands near K remain essentially unaffected, the Γ-point electron pocket—composed primarily of out-of-plane p z orbitals—exhibits a pronounced energy shift. This collective behavior provides definitive evidence for a temperature-driven phase transition with Fermi surface reconstruction. These findings demonstrate that VHSs emerge from band structure extrema and saddle points occur at strategic locations that fundamentally govern optoelectronic response.

VHS-governed exotic phenomena through direct configurations
Our analysis reveals that RVS undergoes significant topological modifications near its T CDW, manifesting as band structure evolution, Fermi surface reconstruction, and pronounced VHS rearrangements. These emergent properties create unprecedented opportunities for low-energy photon detection. Our work demonstrates—for the first time—the direct utilization of kagome-derived topological states for photodetection. We now present the remarkably promising experimental results in photodetection.

We develop the structure of the kagome-metal-based photodetector (Fig. 3a), comprising a bowtie antenna-which serves as electrodes and features a left-right symmetric optical field efficiently coupling photon energy into the channel-and the kagome material RVS. The RVS channel layer is prepared by mechanical exfoliation, and the device is meticulously patterned into a planar configuration. (further details are provided in the Methods). Complete finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulation details are provided in Supplementary Note 5.

The energy distribution curves (EDCs) extracted near the E F region (Fig. 3b) demonstrate the dynamic evolution of the RVS system’s band structure with decreasing temperature (from 130 to 10.5 K). In the normal state (T>T CDW), both VHS1 and VHS2 at the M-point maintain their positions and exhibit minimal temperature dependence. In the CDW state (T<T CDW), the electronic states near the M-point undergo a progressive shift toward higher binding energies with decreasing temperature (further details illustrated in Fig. S7). In kagome systems exhibiting Fermi surface nesting characteristics, these observations provide key insights into the microscopic physical mechanisms underlying electronic instabilities. The VHS exhibits intrinsic electronic instability. Fermi surface nesting facilitates enhanced electron scattering along its characteristic wavevector. Simultaneously, the emergence of a new VHS3 feature leads to a significant amplification of the DOS at the E F. The strongly enhanced DOS at these singularities creates ideal conditions for low-energy photon detection. Figure 3c elucidates the microscopic mechanism governing the enhanced photoresponse, showing that the VHS-induced DOS peak increases the number of available initial states for the optical transition.

Our full-spectrum analysis reveals distinct temperature-dependent photoresponse characteristics of the photodetector across three key THz bands (0.02–0.04, 0.08–0.1, and 0.33–0.355 THz) at 0 mV bias. Figure 3d–f demonstrate that the photoresponse intensity, color-graded from dark to light blue (strongest to weakest), consistently peaks at T CDW ~102 K in all frequency ranges. The top-view schematics (Fig. 3d–f, insets) spatially resolve these response maxima. As the photocurrent intensity exhibits a positive correlation with the DOS, we derive the quantitative relationship expressed in Eq. 1.

J(ω) ∝ e D(E) |⟨f| H^ int |i⟩|² ℏω Φ(ω) (1)

where J(ω) denotes photocurrent density, e represents electron charge, D(E) corresponds to the electronic DOS, ⟨f| H^ int |i⟩ describes transition matrix element incorporating initial state, final state, and perturbation Hamiltonian, ℏω is incident photon energy, Φ(ω) describes incident photon flux. As clearly demonstrated by the simplified Eq. 1, the photocurrent density is directly influenced by the electronic DOS. In the normal state of kagome metal RVS, two VHSs exist near the E F at the high-symmetry M-point. CDW phase transition renormalizes the band structure and new VHS emerges. Since the electronic DOS exhibits logarithmic divergence near VHS, the phase transition therefore enhances the photocurrent density J(ω) through increased D(E).

Under an applied bias of 100 mV, we systematically measured the temperature-dependent photoresponse of the RVS-based detector at 0.03, 0.09, and 0.35 THz (Fig. 3g). Experimental results indicate that at T CDW (~102 K), the device’s photoresponse exhibits significant nonlinear enhancement. Notably, applying a 100 mV bias maintains the peak frequency while significantly enhancing the photocurrent intensity (full spectral scans available in Supplementary Note 8). This enhancement mechanism arises from bias-excited electronic transitions between VHS.

Figure 3h compares the photoresponse enhancement between the normal and CDW phases at a 100 mV bias, revealing frequency-dependent amplification factors of 60.82 × (0.03 THz); 12.64 × (0.1 THz); and 3.18 × (0.35 THz). This enhancement aligns with the theoretical predictions: the phase transition redistributes VHS and modifies the electronic DOS near critical points, thereby amplifying interband transitions. Our results establish kagome materials as a platform for frequency-selective photoresponses through many-body correlations.

The second-order photocurrent (I ph) scaled linearly with the incident electric field power (P in) across temperatures (77–300 K), as shown in Fig. 3i. The photodetector exhibits ideal linearity over more than two orders of magnitude in P in and the data are well fitted with a simple power law (I ph ∝ P in^α, α=0.99±0.005) at all measured temperatures. This temperature-independent nonlinearity is a direct manifestation of the RVS system’s singularelectronic structure, where VHS-derived DOS enhances multiphoton processes. Our results establish kagome materials as a unique platform for wide-temperature-range nonlinear photonics.

Noise is a critical parameter influencing the performance of optoelectronic devices. Once the temperature is below T CDW, the electronic noise spectral density shows a dramatic reduction by over two orders of magnitude (from 3.8×10⁻²³ A²/Hz² to 1.38×10⁻²⁵ A²/Hz²). The system exhibits enhanced stability upon entering the CDW state, with significantly reduced random carrier scattering events. The Noise Equivalent Power (NEP) is a critical parameter. Across the entire modulation frequency range, the device achieves an average NEP of approximately 20 pW/Hz¹/². Operating at 0.1 THz, our device demonstrates ultrafast response characteristics with 580 ns rise time and 520 ns fall time, which is several orders of magnitude faster than other thermoelectric detectors (such as ≈ 170 µs of tellurium nanowire photodetector). (see details in Fig. S12)

VHS-driven heterodyne mixing from millimeter wave to THz band
Based on the unique VHS properties as well as band-renormalization of kagome-metals, we further investigate the potential of heterodyne detection. In our measurements (details can be found in Methods), the fabricated kagome material-based mixer serves as a frequency conversion device in the circuit (Fig. 4a), which constitutes a critical component in modern RF communication systems.

The heterodyne THz detection system, governed by novel physical mechanisms, achieves broadband operation and high detection sensitivity across phase transitions. The schematic illustration of the mixing process under optical beating with in two different frequencies in kagome-based materials is presented in Fig. 4b. The kagome material-based mixer generates distinctive heterodyne signals through coupling of the local oscillator (f LO) and radio frequency (f RF) inputs, yielding an intermediate-frequency beat signal V IF described by:

V IF(t) = L 0(t) R THz(t) = L o R THz/2 * cos(ω LO - ω THz)t + cos(ω LO + ω THz)t (2)

where V IF(t) represents the intermediate frequency output signal, L 0(t) represents the local oscillator signal, R THz(t) represents the radio frequency signal. First, we demonstrate harmonic mixing in a kagome material-based mixer under collimated 6.5 GHz excitation. Through spectrum analysis, the first, second, and third harmonic comb lines are clearly resolved, with the harmonic signals exhibiting robust power dependence. Notably, the generated frequency comb also serves as a tunable local oscillator (f LO), enabling versatile heterodyne mixing. The measured f IF adheres precisely to the expected relationship: f IF = f RF – n f LO (n∈ℕ+) (Figure S14).

Through temperature-dependent measurements, we implement heterodyne mixing techniques in kagome-material-based mixers to systematically investigate their potential for modern communication technologies. Figure 4c demonstrates the temperature evolution of f IF signal arising from the distinctive VHS inherent to kagome systems. To ensure reliable characterization of mixing dynamics within the spectrum analyzer’s bandwidth constraints, we implement a heterodyne scheme using 22.4 GHz (f LO) and 23.4 GHz (f RF) signals. Control experiments with three independent mixers confirmed the reproducibility of our observations. Notably, we observe a pronounced enhancement in f IF signal intensity as the temperature decreased from 300 K to below T CDW. This anomalous behavior originates from temperature-induced modifications in the electronic band structure: (i) the emergence and upward energy shift of a VHS at the M-point, and (ii) the formation of a secondary VHS at the R-point below T CDW. The cooperative migration of these singularities enhances electronic transitions, resulting in the observed macroscopic amplification of the f IF signal.

Kagome systems exhibit exceptional promise for self-mixing applications as noted above. Building on this foundation, we observe broadband multi-wave-mixing in nonlinear kagome systems. Figure 4d demonstrates the characteristic signatures of subharmonic N-wave mixing (WM) (f LO is 23.4 GHz, f RF is 25.4 GHz and f IF signal is precisely captured by the spectrum analyzer). These peaks include three types of spectra: the two fundamental signals (ω₁=2πf LO, ω₂=2πf RF), the f IF signal (f IF = f RF - f LO), their higher-order modes, and the WM components (n f LO ± m f RF, where n, m=1, 2, 3…). The highest observed components reach up to 5 (f RF - f LO) and 6 f LO - 5f RF. These results indicate that, due to the material’s highly complex Fermi surface and exotic electronic behavior below T CDW, a frequency comb-like heterodyne mixing effect can be generated, with higher-order components extending up to the fifth order.

To further investigate the dynamic range of the kagome material-based mixer, the relationship between the f IF signals of different harmonic mixing orders and the incident power (P LO and P RF) is shown in Fig. 4e. The relationship follows the power law, P out = α P in (where P in = P RF), and the solid line represents the slope of the output power measured in the experiment. Notably, even when the f IF signal is set to its lower limit (P RF = -25 dBm, P LO = 14.8 dBm), the f IF signals at (f RF - f LO) and (2f LO - f RF) remain clearly detectable. This indicates that the minimum power excitation threshold of the mixer can be less than -25 dBm, demonstrating the potential of kagome materials for precise carrier frequency information acquisition.

By harnessing the exotic electronic properties of kagome material, we demonstrate the mixing range to the THz band for modern RF communication systems. The f LO is increased to above 100 GHz, approaching the electrical oscillation limit of micron-scale devices. Simultaneously, the f RF is tuned across a range from the Ku and Ka bands to the W band, as shown in Fig. 4f. This shows that the kagome-based device demonstrates intrinsic frequency-agile capture capability, operating across a very wide bandwidth of 1–100 GHz. The conversion loss (CL) increases from 20.1 ± 0.2 dB to 57.5 ± 0.2 dB at 100 GHz. This performance highlights the device’s promising applicability in next-generation wireless communication systems.

The frequency CL, defined as one of the key metrics for mixers, is expressed as:

CL = P in / P out = 10 log (30 P RF / P IF) (3)

where, 30 represents the gain coefficient of the LNA, S λ=λ²/4π represents the diffraction-limited area within the incident wavelength; S represents the area of the waveguide flare. The CL of the mixer near 100 GHz is 57.5 ± 2 dB, while the CL in the RF band is 20 ± 2 dB.

---

## Methods

Crystal growth and characterization
Single crystals of RbV₃Sb₅ were grown via flux-based growth technique. The precursor RbSb was prepared by reacting Rb (purity 99.75%) and Sb granules (purity 99.99%) at 300 °C. Starting materials of RbSb, Sb and V powder (purity 99.99%) were loaded inside a Canfield crucible with a molar ratio of 3:9:1, sealed in a quartz tube. The assembly was heated up to 1100 °C in a furnace within 12 h and kept at this temperature for 10 h. It was subsequently slowly cooled down to 800 °C at a temperature decreasing rate of 50 °C/h and kept for 5 h, and then slowly cooled down further to 450 °C at 2 °C/h. Finally, the assembly was taken out from the furnace and decanted with a centrifuge to separate RbV₃Sb₅ single crystal from the flux. With the exception of sealing and heat treatment procedures, all other preparation processes were conducted in an argon-filled glove box to prevent reaction of Rb with atmospheric oxygen and moisture.

Atomically resolved the scanning transmission electron microscope measurement
The atomic arrangement was examined using a double aberration-corrected Thermo Scientific Spectra 300 STEM (Thermo Scientific, USA), operating at 300 kV with a convergence angle of 25 mrad and a collection angle ranging from 70 to 250 mrad. HAADF STEM images were acquired with a dwell time of 10 s per pixel.

Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy measurement
ARPES was used to characterize kagome metal RbV₃Sb₅ samples. The ARPES measurements were conducted at the BL-03U beamline of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility, using a Scienta Omicron DA30 analyzer. The photon energy is 86 eV. The energy and angular resolutions were set to better than 50 meV and 0.02 Å⁻¹, respectively. Samples were cleaved in situ under ultrahigh vacuum conditions, revealing flat and mirror-like (100) surfaces. During measurements, the temperature was maintained at T~9 K, and the pressure in the main chamber was kept below 7×10⁻¹¹ torr.

First-principles calculations and theoretical modeling
We performed first-principles calculations using the Vienna ab initio simulation package with the projector augmented-wave method. The exchange-correlation energy was treated with the generalized-gradient approximation functional of Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof. The plane-wave basis was employed with a kinetic-energy cutoff of 600 eV, and the k-space integration was performed with 9×9×4 and 4×4×4 k-meshes for the pristine cell and 2×2×1 supercell, respectively. All atoms were allowed to relax along the calculated forces until all the residual force components were less than 0.001 eV/Å. The calculated lattice parameters of the pristine structure are a=b=5.472 and c=9.073 Å. The spectral function A(k, E F) on the Fermi Surface was computed using WANNIER90 and WANNIERTOOLS, where the maximally localized Wannier functions were constructed by projecting the Bloch states onto V-d and Sb-p atomic orbitals. The phonon spectrum for the pristine phase was calculated using the finite displacement method with 3×3×4 k-points and a 3×3×1 supercell.

Device fabrication
Under room temperature conditions, optoelectronic devices were fabricated through mechanical exfoliation. The high-quality RbV₃Sb₅ sample was mechanically exfoliated onto blue tape (Shanghai Onway Technology Co., Ltd) and then directly transferred onto a high-resistivity silicon (ρ=20,000 Ω·cm) substrate coated with a thin SiO₂ oxide layer (300 nm), resulting in an RbV₃Sb₅ thin film. The antenna structure was patterned, and the contact area was defined using electron beam lithography, followed by etching. Cr/Au was deposited onto the material via electron beam evaporation to establish the electrical contact. The optoelectronic detector was fabricated following the metal lift-off process.

Performance measurement
The electrical characteristics of the detector at room temperature were obtained using a Keithley 4200A-SCS Parametric Analyzer. For optical measurements, the THz frequency was tuned to 0.30 THz (WR 2.8 tripler) and 0.12 THz (WR 9 tripler) using a VDI multiplier connected to a 40 GHz microwave source (Agilent E8257D). The optical response was modulated with a TTL signal at a frequency of 1 kHz and recorded using an oscilloscope, after passing through a low-noise voltage preamplifier (SR570) and a lock-in amplifier (SR830). The power density of the THz radiation was measured using a commercially calibrated photomixing THz power meter (TK100), with measurements taken at 2.5, 1, and 1 mW cm⁻² for frequencies of 0.04, 0.12, and 0.30 THz, respectively.

Heterodyne-mixing characterizations
A heterodyne is a signal frequency that is created by combining or mixing two other frequencies using a signal processing technique called heterodyning, which was invented by Canadian inventor-engineer Reginald Fessenden. Heterodyne mixing can be understood by analogy to musical beats-when two slightly different musical notes are played simultaneously, we hear a pulsating ‘beat’ at the difference frequency between them. Similarly, in heterodyne mixing, two signals at different frequencies (local oscillator and radio frequency) are combined in a nonlinear device (the mixer), producing new signals at the sum (f RF + f LO) and difference (|f RF - f LO|) frequencies. In our measurements, the fabricated mixer (kagome material-based detector) serves as a frequency conversion device within the circuit (Fig. 4a), constituting a critical component in modern RF communication systems. The differential frequency (referred to as the intermediate frequency) is selectively utilized because it enables easier electronic processing compared to the original high-frequency signal.

The mixing system at cryogenic temperature primarily consists of two major modules: the heterodyne mixing optical path and the cryogenic temperature refrigeration system. As shown in the lower-left part of the Fig. 4a, the system includes essential components for modern wireless communication—the f LO signal and the heterodyne f RF signal. The f LO signal is collimated using a TPX (polymethylpentene) lens with a focal length of 100 mm and directed onto a beam splitter. The f RF signal is incident on the beam splitter via an off-axis parabolic mirror (OAP), which focuses the millimeter-wave/THz beam. The optical signal is then precisely combined and directed onto the mixer after passing through the Dewar window (Sapphire). Different frequency bands requires specific THz sources. For microwave mixing in the 0–67 GHz range, a microwave source (Agilent E8257D, 0.02–0.04 THz) and a vector network analyzer (Ceyear) are used to provide the f LO and f RF signals, respectively. For the mixing configuration in the 0.08–0.12 THz range, the Agilent E8257D microwave source (0.02–0.04 THz) is connected to a VDI multiplier (WR 9.0) and a 100 GHz source (TeraSense). The f IF is fed into a LNA (ultra wide band=0.01–20 GHz, gain=30 dB Typ, noise figure=2.5 dB). The amplified f IF signal was then measured using a spectrum analyzer (0–27 GHz). Meanwhile, the other path of the optical signal passing through the beam splitter is accurately directed onto a TK power meter to calibrate the optical power. The right half of the figure depicts the low-temperature refrigeration module, which comprises a 77 K Closed Cycle Cryogenic System manufactured by Shanghai Lind Precision Instruments Limited.

In the higher-order harmonic mixing section, the f LO signal is used to generate higher-order harmonics signals (n f LO, where n ranges from 1 to 6) at the point of incidence. These generated signals are then mixed with another RF signal to produce an IF signal, denoted as (n f LO - f RF).

Data availability
Relevant data generated in this study are provided in the article and Supplementary Information. All raw data that support the plots within this paper and other findings of this study are available from the corresponding authors upon request.
